data.name: The Long Winter
data.description: Three people have died in nine days, in three districts, with nothing in common except that all five of them signed one authorisation during the border winter. Two names are left on that page, and one of them is yours to protect.
data.successDescription: The village bought four convoys of grain across a closed border and paid for three. Not because anyone decided to cheat him. Because the paperwork was built so that nobody would ever have to know his name.

objectives.description:
A rank, pinned on the wall behind the desk. A protection detail.

You are in the briefing room before you have been told who you are protecting.

She puts a list on the table. Five names. Three struck through.

"Three dead in nine days, in three districts. No connection anyone can see, except that all five of these signed one authorisation during the border winter."

"Your principal is the fifth signature. She is a serving officer of the requisition bureau. She does not want a detail, and that is not her decision."

"Grain. The border had been shut for a year, and this village was three weeks away from eating its seed stock."

"You cannot buy food across a closed border. Not as a village. Every crossing has a checkpoint, and every checkpoint keeps a book of names."

"So the bureau hired people who do not have a village. There is nothing a checkpoint can hold over a man who has already lost everything he could be threatened with."

Four crossings were contracted. Four convoys of grain, brought over in the dark and written into the books as local cartage, because that is the only way they could be written down at all.

Three payments went out. The fourth was authorised, held, and returned to the treasury by an officer who wrote one word in the margin.

"Concluded."

The fourth name on the list is not struck through. He is a serving deputy, and he has not been at his desk in nine days.
Four places worth a day, and the man doing this has spent nine days proving he is not in a hurry.

nextObjectiveId.text: The three who are already dead.

objectives.description: Three houses in three districts, and the relief team has left all of them exactly as found.

No forced entry. Nothing taken. A cold pot on a stove, and a chair pushed back.

Each of them let somebody in, and sat down opposite them.

Three afternoons to learn that a man who is invited in does not leave marks.
The bureau keeps border winter requisitions under seal, and your principal's name is on the short list that can break it.

The requisition file is perfect, and every line of it is a lie about where the grain came from. Local cartage, local depots, local carters who do not exist.

Four deliveries. Not three.

The fourth came in during the last week of the famine and was signed for at a relief depot by a clerk who had never heard of the contract. No counterparty. No name. Nothing to join it to anything.

The village ate all four. It paid for three.
You take the street outside the principal's house for an evening, on the theory that he will come to her.

Nobody comes.

Halfway through the second hour, she opens her front door, looks directly at where you are standing, and closes it again.

By morning there will be a complaint on a desk about the watcher outside her house. She will write a very exact complaint.
The fourth signature is not at his desk. You work the coach yards until you find him. Sixty one years old, two bags, a coach ticket in his coat.

He is not arguing about being escorted. He is arguing about being escorted back into the village.

"I am the fourth of five, and I intend to be somewhere else when he reaches the fifth."

He looks past you at the yard gate, and stops talking entirely.

Two come through the gate at a walk. They do not look at you. They look at the man with the bags.

One of them puts a hand out, palm up.
objectives.drawDescription: The battle ended in a draw
objectives.failDescription: You failed to defeat the opponent

objectives.description:
They are patient and unhurried, and they put you down without haste.

What saves the ledger is the coach yard filling with morning. Carters, grooms, witnesses. They do not work in front of a crowd. They withdraw, and the deputy has not moved from the wheel.

There is a ledger in the second bag. Not an official one.

"They were not here for me. They were here for that. They would have killed me for it, and I want you to understand those are different things."

Four crossings. Three receipts. The fourth authorised and returned.

He has kept his own copy for eleven years, because he was the one who countersigned the third payment, and he knew what a missing fourth would eventually mean.

On the last page, added within the month, in a hand that is not his: a place, and an hour.

Your principal reads six pages standing, and sits down for the seventh.

"I signed it. I was twenty six, it was the third day of a famine, and I would sign it again."

She puts a finger on the margin note.

"I did not write that. I know why it was written, which is worse."

"The crew that carried the contract was taken on the far side, between the third crossing and the fourth. We heard it within the week. Nobody came to collect, the drop stayed full, and the famine broke, and the emergency cartage that hid the first three payments stopped running. There was no longer anything to hide a fourth payment inside."

"So an officer looked at a file with a dead counterparty and no name in it, and wrote the word that closed it. It was defensible. It was cheap. Both of those were true at once, and that is how these things are always done."

She turns the ledger around so you can see the fourth line.

"Except that the fourth convoy arrived. Somebody brought it through after the crew was gone. And the file was built so that no one would ever have to know his name, which means no one ever had to notice that he was owed."

"Then he has sent an invoice, and I am going to answer it. The alternative is that he keeps working down a page that ends with me."

She takes her coat off the hook.

"If it goes badly, your job is not to win it. Your job is that I leave."

A drying yard on the north cut. He set the hour, and he will keep it until the invoice is answered.

Three ways to arrive at it.

nextObjectiveId.text: At the hour, just the two of you.
Four hours early, with the walls covered.
Send her nowhere. Go in her place.

objectives.description: You bring her up the north cut at the hour with nothing in your hands, and hold the mouth of the yard a while before you walk her into it.

The yard is empty except for one figure sitting on the weighing platform, a case beside him. He does not stand when you arrive.

The mask is full and black, and he does not take it off. He looks at her for a while before he says anything.

"Three of five. You will want to tell me that was unnecessary. Save it. I know exactly how necessary it was, which is not very."

You tell him he could have sent that number to the bureau instead of into three houses.

"To which name? Hers is on a door. Mine is on nothing."

He sounds like a man reading a column of figures.

"The crew died on the far side of the third crossing. I brought the fourth one over on my own, eleven nights, and your depot signed for it and gave the carter a bowl of soup."

"Then I stood at a drop for four months. A bureau can send a bill to a person. A person cannot send a bill to a bureau. That is the whole arrangement, and this village has been enjoying it since the winter it stopped paying."

nextObjectiveId.text: Then we do this the other way.

objectives.description:
He waits, and when you do not fill the silence, he goes on.

"Nobody lets me finish. They start explaining that it was a long time ago. As though the length of it were mine to carry."

He sets the invoice on the platform between you.

"Four crossings. I made the last one alone, after the others were taken, because a contract does not stop being a contract when your crew is dead."

"It has been eleven years. I am aware. I have carried the interest."

nextObjectiveId.text: Then we do this the other way.

objectives.description: You take the yard four hours before his hour, put people on the weighbridge and the north wall, and take the wall yourself.

He arrives exactly at the hour anyway, walking up the open cut with the case in one hand.

He stops at the gate, counts, and sets the case down where it can be seen.

Then he keeps walking. The three who came up behind him do not.
He does not argue, and he does not ask why. He looks at the number of people in the yard, and understands that a bureau has answered an appointment with an ambush.
objectives.drawDescription: The battle ended in a draw
objectives.failDescription: You failed to defeat the opponent

objectives.description:
He empties everything you were holding, and then starts on what you were standing behind.

You get her off the north cut. The case is still on the gravel where he set it down, and nobody has touched it.
You put her in the bureau with the door locked, and take the north cut alone, an hour early. You give the yard a long look before you walk into it.

He is already on the weighing platform. He watches you come the whole way across, and does not stand.

"She is not coming."

It is not a question, and there is nothing in it you could call surprise.

"Then you have made this simpler and worse. Simpler, because I will not have to look at her. Worse, because you have decided, on her behalf, that this is a thing to be handled rather than answered."

nextObjectiveId.text: She signed it at twenty six. I did not.

objectives.description:
You tell him the truth of it. She signed at twenty six. You signed nothing.

"I know what she was. I have read the authorisation more often than she has."

He opens the case anyway, to nobody, because the person it was opened for is behind a locked door across the district.

"Four convoys. Three payments. I brought the last one through alone and nobody in your village has ever known that, because nobody was ever supposed to know anything."

"Take it to her. Tell her I did the correct thing, and came to the meeting."

nextObjectiveId.text: Then we do this the other way.

objectives.description:
He stands unhurried, and the first thing he does is take away everything you prepared.

Whatever you were holding is gone in the opening exchange, and what is left is you, without the things you were counting on.
objectives.drawDescription: The battle ended in a draw
objectives.failDescription: You failed to defeat the opponent

objectives.description:
He removes what you brought, and then takes his time about the rest.

When it is over he has not moved from the platform, and the invoice is still lying on it, where he put it.

The case holds the invoice, three receipted instalments, and a copy of a margin note in an officer's hand.

Concluded.

Underneath it, a relief depot's receiving slip from the last week of the famine. Grain, signed for, no counterparty named. The fourth convoy.

He has carried the village's own paperwork, in better order than the bureau's, and brought it to the meeting.

"Payment. That word means what it says, and it always did. Four crossings. Three quarters is not a discount."

The quarter is paid out of a discretionary line, into an account that closes the same afternoon. No name at either end. Entered as cartage.

Your principal signs it herself rather than send it up.

"Two names are still on that page, and both of them are alive."

She blots it.

"And I have just written down, in my own hand, that this office pays when it is pressed hard enough. Somebody will find that entry one day, and it will be a very bad afternoon for whoever is sitting here."

nextObjectiveId.text: Paid, and written down in her own hand.

objectives.description:
The ledger, the invoice, and the margin note go up in one envelope, with your report attached.

It comes back in eleven days, with no decision on it, and a note asking whether the matter is closed operationally.

"Closed operationally."

She reads the phrase several times.
